items.title: [Real Estate 101 #3] You Never Really Buy a House — You Buy a Bundle of Rights
items.body:
> A deed transfers rights, not dirt: ownership is a bundle of legal powers, other people can hold slices of that bundle, and the county recorder's office is where the world finds out who holds what.

## Today's Concept

Ask someone what they own after closing and they'll point at a building. Lawyers point at something less photogenic: a **bundle of rights**. Classic American property law describes ownership as the right to *possess*, *use*, *exclude* others, *enjoy* the benefits, and *transfer* the whole thing to someone else.

The largest bundle has a name — **fee simple absolute**. It's ownership with no time limit and no strings attached, and it's what most U.S. homebuyers get.

But the bundle can be split, and that's where things get interesting. Someone else can hold a right to *use* your land without owning it:

- **Easement** — a right to cross or use part of your land for a specific purpose. The power company's line along your back fence, or a neighbor's shared driveway.
- **Lease (leasehold estate)** — a tenant holds exclusive possession for a set term; you keep the underlying ownership.
- **Life estate** — someone has the right to live there for the rest of their life, after which it passes to a named person.
- **Mortgage lien** — your lender holds a claim against the property until the loan is paid.

Every one of these is a real, enforceable interest in *your* property. You can own a house in fee simple and still not be allowed to build a shed over the utility easement.

Which raises the practical question: how does a buyer ever know what's attached to a property?

The U.S. answer is the **recording system**. Every county has a recorder of deeds (or register of deeds, or county clerk — the name varies). Deeds, mortgages, easements, liens, and judgments get filed there, in public, searchable by property.

Here's the part people get wrong. **Recording doesn't create your ownership.** A signed and delivered deed transfers title between the two parties whether or not anyone files it. What recording does is give the world *constructive notice* — legal notice that you have an interest, whether anyone actually reads the file or not — and that notice sets **priority** when claims conflict.

State **recording acts** decide who wins. Most states use a *notice* or *race-notice* rule: a later buyer who pays value and doesn't know about the earlier deed can beat the earlier buyer who never recorded (and under race-notice, must also record first). A small handful of states use a pure *race* rule — first to record wins, period.

This is the key difference from many countries, including Korea, Germany, and Australia, which use **title registration**: a government register that itself constitutes ownership and is guaranteed by the state. The U.S. mostly records *documents*, not *title*. The county tells you what was filed; it doesn't promise the filings are valid. That gap is exactly why the American closing process has two things other systems barely need: a **title search** and **title insurance**.

## In Everyday Life

Say you're buying a $450,000 three-bedroom in Mesa, Arizona.

Under contract, a title company pulls the chain of title at the Maricopa County Recorder's Office and hands you a preliminary title report. Buried in Schedule B are the exceptions — the slices of the bundle you are *not* getting:

- a 10-foot utility easement across the rear of the lot (so the planned casita gets moved forward);
- CC&Rs recorded by the HOA in 1998, limiting exterior paint colors and RV parking;
- a mechanic's lien for $8,400 filed by a roofer the seller never paid.

The lien has to be paid off at closing — escrow handles it from the seller's proceeds. The easement and the CC&Rs are permanent; they came with the land and they'll pass to whoever buys it from you.

At closing you sign, the deed is delivered, and the title company records it. You also pay a one-time **owner's title insurance** premium — commonly a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars depending on state and price — which covers you if a defect nobody found shows up later: a forged signature in the 1970s, an unknown heir, a misindexed lien. Your lender requires its own separate policy protecting only the loan balance.

Three years later, a woman claims her ex-husband forged her name on a deed in 2009. The recording system didn't prevent that; the insurance is what pays for the defense. That's the American system in one sentence: **public records plus private insurance, doing the job a state guarantee does elsewhere.**

## 3-Line Recap

1. Ownership is a bundle of rights (possess, use, exclude, enjoy, transfer), and full ownership is called fee simple absolute.
2. Other parties can hold slices of that bundle — easements, leases, life estates, liens — and those slices bind whoever buys next.
3. The U.S. records documents rather than registering title, so recording sets priority and gives public notice, while title search and title insurance cover the risk that remains.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**1.** An unrecorded deed is legally void between the seller and the buyer. (O / X)

**2.** Your neighbor has a recorded easement to drive across the edge of your lot. You buy the property; then you sell it five years later. What happens to the easement?
  (a) It ends when you take ownership
  (b) It ends when you sell to the next buyer
  (c) It stays with the land and binds the new owner
  (d) It only stays if the new buyer signs a fresh agreement

**3.** What does an owner's title insurance policy primarily protect against?
  (a) Storm and fire damage to the structure
  (b) Losing money if the buyer's loan is denied
  (c) Ownership defects and undisclosed claims arising before you bought
  (d) The property declining in market value

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Fee simple absolute** — the largest ownership interest in U.S. law: unlimited in duration, with no conditions attached.
- **Easement** — a non-possessory right to use someone else's land for a defined purpose, such as utility access or a shared driveway.
- **Life estate** — the right to possess and use a property for the duration of a person's life, after which it passes to a designated party.
- **Constructive notice** — the legal presumption that the public is aware of a properly recorded document, whether or not anyone actually read it.
- **Recording act** — the state statute that decides which competing claim wins, generally under a race, notice, or race-notice rule.
- **Title insurance** — a one-time-premium policy covering losses from title defects that existed before the purchase.

---

*Answers: 1. X — a signed and delivered deed is fully valid between the two parties; recording protects you against third-party claims and sets priority, but it isn't what makes the transfer real. 2. (c) — a recorded easement appurtenant runs with the land, so it survives every sale until it is formally released or terminated. 3. (c) — title insurance is backward-looking: it covers defects, forgeries, unknown heirs, and missed liens that predate your purchase, not future physical damage or market losses.*

items.title: [MSEC 2025] The Machine Already Knows What It's About to Cut — Inside the Digital Twin That Watches a Milling Machine in Real Time
items.body:
> A machining "digital twin" simulates the cut a fraction of a second before it happens, then compares that prediction against the machine's own live data — turning a blind metal-cutting process into one that can sense tool wear, catch a breaking tool, and duck out of destructive vibration on its own.

## What Was Presented

At the co-located ASME International Manufacturing Science and Engineering Conference (MSEC 2025) and the 53rd NAMRI/SME North American Manufacturing Research Conference — held at Clemson University's Greenville, SC campus, June 23–27, 2025 — **Yusuf Altintas**, Distinguished University Scholar at the University of British Columbia and head of its Manufacturing Automation Laboratory, delivered a keynote on **digital twin assisted machine tool monitoring**.

The problem he addressed is deceptively simple. When a CNC milling machine carves a jet engine bracket or a mold cavity out of a solid metal block, nobody can actually see the cut. The contact zone is buried under a flood of coolant and a spray of hot chips. The cutting edge is spinning thousands of times per minute. By the time an operator notices something is wrong — a scorched surface, a ruined part, a snapped cutter — the damage is already paid for.

Altintas's answer is to run a **virtual copy of the cut alongside the real one**. The virtual model knows the toolpath, the geometry of the cutter, and the shape of the raw stock, so at every instant it can compute the **cutter–workpiece engagement (CWE)**: exactly which slice of the cutting edge is buried in metal, and how much. The virtual tool position is kept synchronized with the real tool position as it travels along the toolpath, so simulated and measured states line up moment to moment.

That predicted engagement is then **fused with two streams of live data**: internal signals the CNC controller already produces (notably spindle motor current, plus axis positions and feed), and signals from external sensors such as accelerometers or an instrumented tool holder. The keynote showed three applications built on that fusion:

- **Adaptive cutting-load control** — the feed rate is adjusted on the fly to hold cutting forces at a safe target, using either directly measured forces or forces reconstructed from an accelerometer-integrated tool holder.
- **Tool wear and breakage detection** — spindle current is normalized by the engagement area from the virtual model, which strips out the "the cut just got bigger" effect and leaves the part of the signal that actually reflects a dulling or broken edge.
- **Chatter detection and avoidance** — chatter, a violent self-excited vibration between tool and part, is identified from the frequency spectrum of the spindle motor current after compensating for the dynamics of the drive train, and the machine changes conditions to escape it.

The through-line is that a raw sensor signal is ambiguous, but a sensor signal *interpreted against a physics-based prediction of what should be happening* is not.

## Why It Matters

Most "smart factory" monitoring today works by learning from data alone: record thousands of good cuts, flag anything that looks different. That works — until the next job uses a different cutter, a different material, or a different toolpath, and the model has to be retrained from scratch. High-value machining is mostly small batches and one-offs, which is exactly the regime where pure data-driven monitoring struggles most.

A physics-based digital twin sidesteps that. Because the twin computes engagement from geometry and cutting mechanics, it can tell a *normal* current spike (the tool just entered a thicker section of metal) from an *abnormal* one (the tool is worn) on a part it has never seen before. That's the difference between a system that needs a training run and one that works on the first part.

The practical stakes are concrete. Aerospace and mold-making parts can represent weeks of accumulated machining time in a single block of titanium or hardened steel; a tool that breaks at hour 30 can scrap all of it. Chatter, meanwhile, is the reason many shops run conservatively slow — machinists back off feeds and speeds to stay away from vibration they can't predict. Monitoring that reliably detects and avoids chatter lets a machine run closer to its real limits instead of a safety margin guessed by experience.

There's a broader point too. This is a counterweight to the assumption that more sensors and bigger models are the path to autonomous manufacturing. Altintas's architecture argues that the decisive ingredient is a *model of the process* that tells you what the sensors should be reading — and that a modest sensor set plus good physics beats a rich sensor set with no physics.

## An Easy Way to Understand It

Think of a car's fuel gauge versus its trip computer.

A bare fuel gauge tells you consumption is high right now. It can't tell you whether that's because you're climbing a mountain pass or because a tire is going flat — same reading, completely different meaning.

A trip computer that knows the route, the grade of the road, and the car's weight can predict what consumption *should* be for this stretch of highway. Now the same reading becomes diagnostic: if you're burning 20% more than the prediction on flat ground, something is genuinely wrong.

The digital twin is the trip computer for a cutting tool. Spindle current alone is the bare gauge. Spindle current divided by the engagement area the twin predicted is the diagnostic:

```
wear indicator ≈ measured spindle current ÷ predicted engagement area
```

Take the geometry out of the signal, and what's left is the health of the tool.

## Three-Line Recap

1. A virtual model of the cut runs in step with the real machine and predicts, instant by instant, how much of the cutter is engaged in metal.
2. That prediction is fused with the CNC's own internal data and external sensor signals to control cutting force, track tool wear and breakage, and detect chatter vibration.
3. Because the twin is grounded in the physics of cutting rather than in training data from past jobs, it can monitor parts the system has never machined before.

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Digital twin** — A live virtual model of a physical process, kept synchronized with the real thing so predictions and measurements can be compared moment to moment.
- **CNC (Computer Numerical Control)** — The controller that drives a machine tool's motors along a programmed toolpath; it also generates internal data such as motor current and axis position.
- **Cutter–workpiece engagement (CWE)** — The instantaneous geometry of contact between the rotating cutter and the material: which part of the edge is cutting, and how deeply.
- **Chatter** — Self-excited vibration between tool and workpiece that grows on its own, leaving wavy surface marks and damaging tools and spindles.
- **Adaptive control** — Automatically adjusting machining parameters (typically feed rate) in real time to hold a target such as cutting force, rather than running fixed values programmed in advance.

items.title: A Crypto Rulebook Runs Out of Calendar: The CLARITY Act's Last Days Before Recess
items.body:
*This article is a general explainer on pending U.S. legislation, based on publicly available congressional records and mainstream news reporting. Legislative schedules change quickly — verify the current status of any bill before relying on it. Nothing here is investment, legal, or tax advice.*

---

Washington runs on deadlines it sets for itself, and the one now pressing on the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act is a simple line on a calendar: the Senate's August state work period, scheduled to begin around **August 10**.

Nothing legally expires that day. No provision sunsets, no bill dies. But a chamber that leaves town without moving a bill has, in practical terms, told you something about that bill's priority — and about the arithmetic waiting for it in the fall. For what would be America's first comprehensive crypto **market-structure** law, the days before recess have become the whole story.

## What the CLARITY Act is actually trying to do

Start with the problem it addresses, because "crypto regulation" is a phrase that hides more than it explains.

The United States already regulates digital assets. It just does so through a patchwork of enforcement actions, decades-old case law, and two agencies with overlapping claims. The core question — is a given token a **security** (Securities and Exchange Commission turf) or a **commodity** (Commodity Futures Trading Commission turf)? — has largely been answered one lawsuit at a time.

The CLARITY Act, which passed the House in July 2025 with a substantial bipartisan majority, tries to answer it in statute instead. Broadly, it would:

- **Split jurisdiction by asset type**, routing spot markets in "digital commodities" to the CFTC while leaving investment-contract offerings with the SEC.
- **Create a registration path** for digital asset exchanges, brokers, and dealers, including provisional registration while rules are written.
- **Define a transition test** — often discussed as whether a blockchain has become sufficiently decentralized — that lets an asset move from the securities regime into the commodities regime as its underlying network matures.
- **Set custody, disclosure, and customer-asset-segregation requirements** for intermediaries.

It is the second half of a two-part project. The first half, the stablecoin law enacted in 2025, was the easier lift: narrower subject, clearer analogies to existing payments regulation. Market structure is where the genuinely hard trade-offs live.

## Why the recess date matters more than it looks

Floor time in the Senate is the scarcest resource in American government, and a bill like this consumes a lot of it.

Under normal order, market-structure legislation needs to clear **two committees** — Banking (for the securities side) and Agriculture (which oversees the CFTC) — before it gets a floor slot. It then needs 60 votes to break a filibuster, which means a meaningful bloc of Democratic support, not just party-line agreement. Each of those steps takes days the Senate does not have many of.

The competing demands are familiar. Appropriations deadlines arrive in the fall with a hard edge that crypto policy does not have. Nominations consume floor time continuously. And in an election year, the window for anything requiring sustained cross-party negotiation narrows sharply after Labor Day, as members redirect attention toward campaigns and toward votes that are easier to explain at home.

That's the real mechanism behind the "past 2026" warning. If the bill doesn't have a negotiated text before recess, it returns in September into a shorter, more crowded calendar with less appetite for compromise. And bills that don't pass in a Congress don't carry over — they start again from introduction in the next one, with a possibly different committee balance and a re-litigated text.

## Fight one: ethics rules for officeholders who hold tokens

The first unresolved issue is not about market plumbing at all. It's about who in government may own, issue, or promote digital assets.

Several Democratic negotiators have pressed for conflict-of-interest provisions — variously drafted to cover the President, Vice President, members of Congress, senior executive branch officials, and in some versions their immediate families — restricting the issuance or sponsorship of digital assets while in office. Public reporting through 2025 and 2026 has tied the intensity of this demand to the crypto ventures associated with the President's family, and supporters describe it as a straightforward extension of existing financial conflict rules to a new asset class.

Republican negotiators have generally argued the opposite: that ethics rules are a separate subject from market structure, that folding them in converts a technical bill into a political one, and that any such provisions belong in standalone legislation.

Both positions are internally coherent, which is exactly why the fight is hard. It isn't a drafting disagreement that a good staff lawyer can resolve overnight. It's a disagreement about what the bill is for — and for some Democrats, the ethics language has become the price of the votes needed to reach 60.

## Fight two: illicit finance

The second issue is more technical and, in some ways, harder.

Everyone in the debate agrees that sanctions evasion, ransomware payments, and laundering through digital assets are real problems. The disagreement is about where obligations should attach.

Traditional anti-money-laundering law is built around **intermediaries**: a bank, a broker, an exchange — an entity that knows its customers and can file reports. Decentralized finance complicates that model. When software runs autonomously and no one holds customer funds, it is genuinely unclear who the regulated party is supposed to be.

Two camps have formed. One wants to extend Bank Secrecy Act–style obligations further into the digital asset stack, arguing that a regime with structural gaps invites use of those gaps. The other wants explicit protection for developers of non-custodial software — the position that publishing code isn't operating a money transmitting business — warning that broad liability would push development offshore without meaningfully deterring sophisticated bad actors.

Related questions ride along: how to treat mixing services, what to do about privacy-preserving technologies with both legitimate and illegitimate uses, and how much new authority Treasury should receive.

None of these have obvious compromise landing zones, and unlike the ethics fight, they can't be resolved by simply deciding whether a section stays in or comes out.

## What passing — or not — would actually change

It's worth being precise about the stakes, because both sides of the debate have incentives to overstate them.

**If it passes:** firms gain a registration path and a defined regulator, which mainly affects institutional participants deciding how much compliance risk a U.S. business carries. It would not eliminate volatility, fraud, or loss. Implementation would still take years of agency rulemaking after enactment.

**If it stalls:** the current regime continues — meaning agency policy, enforcement discretion, and litigation outcomes remain the operative rulebook, and can shift with each administration. That instability is the specific thing the industry says it wants fixed, and the specific thing skeptics say is preferable to a framework they consider too permissive.

Neither outcome is a verdict on any particular asset's value. Legislation shapes who supervises a market; it does not underwrite it.

## What to watch in the next few days

A handful of concrete signals will tell you more than any headline:

1. **Does a joint Banking–Agriculture text appear?** A single released draft with both committees' names on it is the clearest evidence real negotiation succeeded.
2. **Is a markup noticed?** Committees post hearing and markup notices in advance. No notice before recess means no committee action before September.
3. **Do the Democratic negotiators issue a statement?** Whether the group that has been negotiating describes talks as ongoing or stalled is the most direct read on whether 60 votes are reachable.
4. **Is the ethics language in a separate vehicle?** If conflict-of-interest provisions get spun into a standalone bill, that's the shape a compromise would most likely take.
5. **Does leadership commit floor time for the fall?** A scheduling commitment survives recess; a general expression of support usually doesn't.

## The unglamorous conclusion

Big legislation rarely fails because someone loses an argument. It fails because the calendar closes while the argument is still running.

The CLARITY Act cleared the harder-looking chamber more than a year ago with bipartisan support. What it faces now isn't ideological opposition so much as arithmetic: two genuinely unresolved policy fights, two committees of jurisdiction, a 60-vote threshold, and a shrinking number of legislative days before an election year absorbs whatever is left.

That may still be enough. Congress has done more in less time when leadership decided a bill would move. But the honest read, as the Senate approaches its August departure, is that the outcome depends less on the merits of the framework than on whether two negotiating teams can close two hard gaps in a very small number of working days — and, failing that, whether anyone still has the appetite to pick it up again in September.

---

*Sources for the underlying legislative record include the Congressional Record, committee announcements, and contemporaneous coverage by major financial news outlets. This summary reflects publicly reported information and does not constitute financial, legal, or tax advice. Readers should consult primary sources and qualified professionals before making any decisions.*

items.title: Your Power Bill Is Now Partly an AI Bill: Inside the Auction That Prices America's Data Center Boom
items.body:
Most people will never read a capacity auction report. But if you live in one of the 13 states or the District of Columbia served by the PJM Interconnection — roughly 65 million people, from Chicago to Newark to Richmond — one line in that report has more influence over your next electricity bill than almost anything happening in your own house.

That line is the clearing price. For the delivery year that runs June 1, 2026 through May 31, 2027, it came in at **$329.17 per megawatt-day** — the effective ceiling allowed in the auction. Two delivery years earlier, the comparable price was **$28.92**.

That is not a typo, and it is not inflation. It is the price of promising that the lights stay on in a grid where demand has started growing again after roughly two decades of sitting flat — and where the fastest-growing single category of new demand is the data center.

## The three numbers that tell the story

| Delivery year | RTO-wide clearing price | Approximate total capacity cost |
|---|---|---|
| 2024 / 2025 | $28.92 per MW-day | ~$2.2 billion |
| 2025 / 2026 | $269.92 per MW-day | ~$14.7 billion |
| 2026 / 2027 | $329.17 per MW-day (at the cap) | ~$16.1 billion |

The 2026/27 auction, whose results PJM published in late July 2025, secured roughly 134,300 megawatts of capacity — a reserve margin somewhere near 19%, comfortably above the target. In other words, the system did not come up short. It simply became far more expensive to keep it that way.

## What a capacity auction actually is

This is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that matters.

Electricity markets pay for two different things. One is **energy** — the actual kilowatt-hours you use, priced more or less continuously. The other is **capacity** — a standing commitment from a power plant, a demand-response aggregator, or a battery to be available and deliver during the worst hours of the year: the January morning when everything is frozen, the July afternoon when everything is running.

PJM buys that commitment years ahead through the Base Residual Auction. Suppliers offer to be available; PJM buys until it has enough to meet a reliability requirement; and — this is the crucial mechanic — **every cleared supplier gets paid the same clearing price**, set by the most expensive offer needed to fill the requirement. Not their own asking price. The market price.

That single design choice is why the number moves so violently. When the requirement rises past the cheap, already-built supply and starts reaching into the expensive tail of the offer stack, the price for *everything* resets upward at once. A modest increase in demand can produce a very immodest increase in cost.

Then the cost gets spread. Utilities buy capacity on behalf of their customers and pass the charge through — showing up in the supply or generation portion of your bill, in your state's price-to-compare, or in a competitive supplier's rate. You never see a line item called "capacity auction." You just see a bigger number.

## Why the price hit the ceiling

Three pressures arrived at the same time.

**Supply left.** Coal and older oil- and gas-fired units have been retiring on economics, age, and environmental compliance schedules. Once a plant deactivates, its capacity stops showing up in the auction.

**Replacement is slow.** New solar, wind, storage, and gas projects have to clear interconnection studies, permitting, local approval, financing, and equipment orders. PJM's queue holds a very large volume of proposed projects; the constraint is not developer interest but the pace of study, construction, and delivery. Heavy-duty gas turbines in particular are effectively sold out well into the next decade, with order backlogs at the handful of firms that build them.

**Demand turned upward.** After years of flat load, PJM's forecasts now show substantial peak growth through 2030 — the sharpest revision the region has seen in a generation. Electrification contributes. Manufacturing contributes. But the category driving the revision is large data-center load, concentrated heavily in Northern Virginia and spreading into Ohio, Pennsylvania, Indiana, and Maryland.

Retirements plus slow replacement plus rising demand equals a tighter requirement met by a more expensive offer stack. The auction did what it was designed to do: it printed a very loud price signal.

## How much of this is really AI?

Here the honest answer requires care, because this is where public discussion tends to get sloppy.

PJM's independent market monitor, which analyzes the auction separately from PJM itself, has published assessments attributing the large majority of the recent price increases to growth in large load — data centers above all. Under that analysis, if data-center demand growth were removed from the reliability requirement, the clearing price would be dramatically lower. That is a modeled counterfactual, not a measurement, and reasonable analysts dispute the exact share. But the direction is not seriously contested: data centers are the dominant swing factor.

Two fair counterpoints belong alongside it.

First, data centers do pay. They pay retail tariffs, they pay capacity charges proportional to their contribution to peak, and in many cases they pay for interconnection upgrades directly. They are not receiving free electricity.

Second, the grievance is about **allocation and risk**, not theft. When a uniform clearing price resets because one customer class is adding gigawatts, every other customer — the household, the school district, the machine shop — pays the new price on their existing consumption too. The build-out's cost is socialized across the whole footprint, while the revenue from the build-out is not. That asymmetry, rather than any single company's behavior, is the actual policy problem.

## What this looks like on your bill

PJM's own estimate for the 2026/27 result was an increase in the range of roughly **1.5% to 5% on typical residential bills**, varying by zone — layered on top of the considerably larger increase already working its way through from the prior auction.

Several things make the lived experience messier than that range suggests:

- **Timing varies.** States and utilities procure default supply on different cycles, so the same auction lands in different months and different chunks depending on where you live.
- **Zones differ.** Transmission constraints mean some areas clear above the RTO-wide price, and those customers absorb more.
- **Capacity is only part of the bill.** Transmission investment, distribution rates, and fuel costs move on their own schedules and can pull the total in the same direction at the same time.

If you want your actual number rather than an average, the practical path is your utility's rate filing or price-to-compare notice at your state public utility commission — that document shows the supply cost being passed through, in your zone, for your service class.

## Who is trying to fix it, and how

The response has been unusually fast by energy-regulation standards.

**A price collar.** After Pennsylvania's governor challenged the auction rules at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, PJM and the state reached a settlement that FERC approved: a floor and a ceiling on the clearing price for the 2026/27 and 2027/28 auctions. The ceiling is precisely why 2026/27 stopped at $329.17. Absent that cap, the price would very likely have gone higher — a detail worth remembering when reading the number.

**Faster interconnection for what's needed.** PJM created a fast-track pathway to move a limited slate of projects that add reliable capacity quickly, alongside broader reforms to its interconnection process.

**Making large loads carry their own weight.** This is the most consequential front. Regulators and utilities across the footprint are reworking how very large customers are treated: minimum-demand contracts so a data center pays for most of the capacity it reserves whether or not it uses it, separate rate classes for large loads, collateral and exit provisions, and rules for "bring your own generation" or co-located supply arrangements. Ohio approved a large-load framework along these lines, and similar proceedings have opened elsewhere. FERC has taken up the co-location question for PJM specifically.

**Demand flexibility.** Because the requirement is driven by a handful of peak hours, a data center willing to curtail or shift to on-site generation during those hours reduces the requirement itself. Several operators have signaled willingness; turning that into enforceable, verifiable commitments is the unfinished work.

## What to watch next

- **Subsequent auction results.** Each new Base Residual Auction tests whether new supply and demand-side commitments are arriving fast enough to pull the price off the ceiling — and what happens when the collar's coverage ends.
- **Whether large-load tariffs actually bind.** A rate class only shifts cost if its minimum-take and collateral terms survive negotiation and litigation intact.
- **Real megawatts, not announcements.** Announced generation projects are cheap; steel in the ground and turbines delivered are what changes an auction outcome.
- **Whether load forecasts hold.** Some share of the interconnection requests in the pipeline is speculative or duplicated across utilities. If forecast demand is revised down, the requirement — and the price — follows.
- **Political durability.** Rate increases of this size tend to outlast the technical debate. Legislative intervention in individual states is a live possibility.

## The bottom line

The AI build-out has a price, and part of it is being paid through an obscure auction that most ratepayers have never heard of. There is nothing hidden or improper about the mechanism — the rules are public, the results are published, and the market is doing exactly what a uniform-clearing-price market does when demand outruns cheap supply.

What is genuinely unresolved is who should bear the cost. Right now the answer is largely "everyone on the system, in proportion to their existing usage." Every reform currently in motion is an attempt to change that answer before the next several auctions lock it in.

---

*Figures in this article are drawn from PJM's published Base Residual Auction results, its independent market monitor's public analyses, and filings at FERC and state utility commissions. Auction results and reform proceedings are updated regularly; for the current numbers, consult PJM's posted auction reports and your state commission's docket. Bill impact ranges are estimates and will differ by utility, zone, and service class. This is general information, not investment or legal advice.*

items.title: Won at the Supreme Court, Still Waiting on the Check: Inside the $165 Billion Tariff Refund Nobody Can Collect
items.body:
There is a peculiar kind of legal victory in which you win everything and receive nothing. Somewhere around 330,000 American importers are living in it right now.

Six months after the Supreme Court held, 6–3, that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give any president the authority to impose tariffs, the courts have ordered roughly $165 billion in collected duties returned to the companies that paid them. On paper, that is one of the largest single refund events the U.S. Treasury has ever faced. In practice, most of the businesses entitled to that money have not seen a dollar of it — and a large share of them are still cutting tariff checks every week.

The gap between the ruling and the refund is not a scandal. It is plumbing. But the plumbing is worth understanding, because it explains why a landmark constitutional decision has so far changed far less about the cost of importing goods into the United States than the headline suggested.

## What the Court actually decided

IEEPA, passed in 1977, lets a president declare a national emergency in response to an "unusual and extraordinary threat" originating largely outside the United States, and then take a list of economic actions — among them, the authority to "regulate ... importation."

The government's argument rested on those three words. If you can regulate importation, the reasoning went, you can condition importation on payment of a duty. Emergencies are unpredictable, and Congress wrote the statute broadly on purpose.

The challengers — a group of small importers and a coalition of states, whose cases were consolidated on the way up — made a structural argument instead. The power to lay duties belongs to Congress under Article I. IEEPA never uses the words *tariff*, *duty*, or *tax*. And in nearly fifty years, across administrations of both parties, no president had ever read the statute that way.

The majority sided with the challengers, applying the now-familiar principle that Congress does not hide decisions of vast economic and political significance inside vague or ancillary statutory language. The Court noted something telling: when Congress *has* delegated tariff authority, it has done so deliberately and with guardrails — required investigations, agency findings, rate ceilings, sunset clauses. IEEPA has none of those. The absence of any procedural machinery was treated as evidence that the machinery was never meant to be there.

The dissent argued for deference in the field of foreign affairs, and read "regulate importation" as plainly capacious enough to include a tariff.

One point gets lost in the coverage: the decision is about *which branch* sets tariffs and *under which statute*. It is not a ruling on whether tariffs are wise policy. That distinction explains nearly everything that has happened since.

## Why winning is not the same as being paid

Customs refunds do not work like a court-ordered settlement where a check gets mailed. They work entry by entry, through a system built for correcting individual paperwork errors, not for unwinding a policy applied to tens of millions of shipments.

**Liquidation is the deadline nobody outside the trade world had heard of.** When goods enter the United States, the importer files an entry summary and deposits estimated duties. Months later, Customs and Border Protection "liquidates" the entry — the final, legally binding computation of what was owed. Once an entry liquidates and the protest window closes, it is generally final. Reopening it requires a specific legal hook. Many entries from the tariffs' earliest months liquidated long before the case reached the Supreme Court, and a meaningful slice of the theoretical $165 billion sits behind that door.

**Being right is not the same as being a party.** Court orders run to the parties before the court. Whether relief extends automatically to every importer in the country, or whether each company must file its own protest or suit to claim its share, has been litigated separately — and that secondary fight is where a great deal of the money is currently parked. Importers who filed protective claims early are in a materially better position than those who waited for the news.

**The refund itself is an accounting exercise at enormous scale.** CBP processes tens of millions of entry summaries a year. Each refund has to be matched to a specific entry, a specific line, a specific tariff classification, and often a specific surety bond. Some entries mixed duties that are now void with duties that remain perfectly valid under other statutes. Untangling those lines is manual work, and there is no button that does it.

**Interest accrues, which softens the wait but complicates the math.** Excess deposits generally carry interest from the date of deposit until refund, at rates Treasury resets quarterly. For a company that paid millions in 2025, that is real money — and also a taxable event landing in a different fiscal year than the original expense.

**Appeals and remands keep resetting the clock.** Even after a Supreme Court ruling on the core question, the downstream cases about scope, timing, and eligibility continue to move through the Court of International Trade and the Federal Circuit. Every remand adds months.

## Who actually gets the money

This is the question that produces the most awkward conversations inside companies.

The refund goes to the **importer of record** — the entity legally on the hook to CBP. That is often not the party that ultimately bore the cost. A U.S. distributor that paid the duty and raised its prices has already recovered much of it from customers. A retailer that negotiated delivered-duty-paid terms may have pushed the cost onto a foreign supplier. Some contracts contain explicit tariff-adjustment clauses that now run in reverse; most do not.

The result is a wave of quiet commercial negotiation that has nothing to do with the constitutional question: *who, in this supply chain, owns this receivable?* Companies with clean documentation and well-drafted clauses are resolving it in weeks. Companies without are discovering that a windfall is only a windfall if you can prove it is yours.

## The wall that replaced the wall

Here is the part that surprises people who followed only the headline. For many importers, the total duty burden has not fallen much, because the tariffs did not disappear so much as change legal address.

IEEPA was the fast lane. Everything else is slower, narrower, and procedurally demanding — but it exists, and it has been used.

| Authority | What it requires | Practical constraints |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Section 232** (Trade Expansion Act of 1962) | Commerce Department investigation finding that imports threaten national security | Product-by-product; investigations take months; no statutory rate cap |
| **Section 301** (Trade Act of 1974) | USTR investigation into unfair foreign practices | Country-specific; notice-and-comment; subject to periodic review |
| **Section 201** (Trade Act of 1974) | ITC finding of serious injury to a domestic industry | Temporary safeguard; must phase down over time |
| **Section 122** (Trade Act of 1974) | Balance-of-payments justification | Capped at 15% and 150 days without congressional action |

Section 232 has done most of the work. Because it is organized around product categories rather than countries, rebuilding coverage means running investigations sector by sector — steel and aluminum derivatives, autos and parts, copper, timber and lumber, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and downstream electronics. Each one is a separate proceeding with its own comment docket and its own effective date.

The practical effect for an importer is that a refund for last year's duties can arrive in the same quarter as a new invoice for this year's, on the same product, at a comparable rate, under a different statute. The money is real. The relief is not.

## What it means for the books

Accountants have been unusually vocal about this one. Under U.S. GAAP, gain contingencies generally are not recognized until realized or realizable — so a company cannot simply book its expected refund as an asset because it read a favorable opinion. The original tariffs were typically expensed through cost of goods sold or capitalized into inventory. The refunds, when they land, tend to arrive as a lump in a later period, distorting margins in a quarter that had nothing to do with the shipments in question.

That timing mismatch is why some importers with large confirmed claims still look, on paper, like they are absorbing tariff costs. They are — until the money moves.

## What it means for prices

Prices are famously sticky downward. Costs that got passed to consumers over two years do not reverse on the day a court rules, particularly when replacement duties are landing in the same categories. Where relief has shown up fastest is in goods that fell outside every Section 232 product scope — certain consumer categories, some apparel and household goods, various inputs with no plausible national-security framing. Where it has shown up least is anywhere touching metals, vehicles, electronics, or pharmaceuticals.

## What to watch next

- **The scope litigation.** Whether relief reaches non-parties automatically is worth more, in dollars, than most of the underlying case.
- **The liquidation cutoff rulings.** Courts are being asked whether finality bars claims on entries that liquidated before the decision. This is the single largest variable in the $165 billion estimate.
- **CBP's processing pace.** Refund throughput, not legal entitlement, now sets the calendar for most companies.
- **New Section 232 proceedings.** Each new product scope narrows the practical benefit of the refund for affected importers.
- **Congress.** The decision hands tariff-setting back to the legislature by default. Whether Congress legislates new delegated authority, tightens the existing ones, or does nothing will determine what the next version of this looks like.

## A practical checklist for importers

If your company imported during the affected period, the useful steps are unglamorous:

1. **Pull your entry data.** Identify every entry summary in the window and its liquidation status. You cannot claim what you cannot locate.
2. **Preserve rights on unliquidated entries** through the appropriate protest or post-summary correction channels, with customs counsel, before deadlines pass.
3. **Separate voided duties from valid ones** line by line. Mixed entries are the most common source of rejected claims.
4. **Read your contracts** for tariff pass-through and adjustment clauses, in both directions, before anyone assumes the refund is theirs.
5. **Talk to your auditor early** about recognition timing so the refund does not become a surprise restatement conversation.
6. **Model the replacement duties**, not the old ones. Your forward cost curve depends on Section 232 scopes, not on a case you already won.

## Bottom line

The Supreme Court answered a constitutional question cleanly: an emergency-powers statute that never mentions tariffs does not authorize them. What it could not do is make an administrative system built for correcting individual entry errors process a nationwide reversal quickly, or prevent the executive branch from rebuilding similar duties through statutes that were always available and are now being used.

For 330,000 companies, the ruling converted a cost into a receivable. That is a genuine improvement. It is also a reminder that in trade law, the judgment is the beginning of the process, not the end of it — and that the distance between a court order and a bank deposit is measured in liquidation dates, not in principles.

---

*This article is general information, not legal, tax, or accounting advice. Figures cited are estimates that shift as litigation and refund processing continue. Importers with potential claims should consult licensed customs counsel and their own advisors about their specific entries and deadlines.*

items.title: The Ground Under Naples Has Risen Four and a Half Feet: Inside Campi Flegrei's 40-Year Wake-Up Call
items.body:
On the last day of July, the ground west of Naples moved hard enough to close a working port.

The magnitude 4.7 earthquake that struck the Campi Flegrei caldera on July 31 was, by the reckoning of Italy's national geophysics institute, the strongest tremor the area has produced in roughly four decades. Twenty-six people were reported injured. Around 130 households were emptied while engineers checked walls and stairwells. The port of Pozzuoli — the ferry link to Ischia and Procida, and a piece of ordinary economic infrastructure for tens of thousands of people — was closed for inspection.

Those are the numbers that traveled. But they are not the story. The story is slower, quieter, and considerably stranger: the floor of the caldera has been rising, more or less continuously, for two decades. Since 2005, the ground at the center of the uplift has swelled by more than 140 centimeters — about four and a half feet.

That is not a metaphor. The coastline near Pozzuoli is physically higher than it was when the first iPhone shipped.

## What bradyseism actually is

The phenomenon has a name that predates modern volcanology: *bradyseism*, from the Greek for "slow movement." It describes the gradual rise and fall of the ground surface inside a volcanic caldera, driven not by lava but by pressure — hot fluids, gases, and possibly magma at depth pushing the rock above them upward like a slow hydraulic jack, then letting it settle again.

Campi Flegrei is the textbook case. The Romans built a market at Pozzuoli, the Macellum, whose surviving columns carry a band of holes bored by marine mollusks several meters above the modern floor. Those holes are a tide gauge running two thousand years long. The ground sank below sea level, sat there for centuries, and rose again. Naples has been living on a piston this whole time.

The caldera itself is about 12 to 15 kilometers across, and most of it is not a mountain. It is a shallow bowl of neighborhoods, ports, thermal baths, and highways, partly submerged under the Gulf of Pozzuoli, partly overlapping the western districts of Naples proper. Roughly half a million people live inside it. That density — European, coastal, historic, and built long before anyone modeled seismic loads — is the variable that turns a geophysics problem into a civil-protection problem.

## Why a 4.7 hurts more here

A magnitude 4.7 is not a large earthquake by global standards. In many parts of the world it would rattle dishes and make the local news for one cycle.

Campi Flegrei is different for two reasons.

**The quakes are extremely shallow.** Most caldera seismicity here originates within a few kilometers of the surface, some of it much shallower than that. Energy that would dissipate through the crust on its way up from a 30-kilometer hypocenter instead arrives almost immediately, concentrated under a small area. The shaking is sharp, loud, and disproportionate to the magnitude number.

**The buildings have been strained for years, not seconds.** This is the point most easily lost. Uplift does not merely precede earthquakes; it deforms structures directly. A masonry building whose foundation has tilted and stretched a few centimeters over a decade is not the same building it was — it has accumulated cracks, lost stiffness, and shed some of its margin. When the sharp shock finally arrives, it lands on a structure already partway through its budget. That is why local damage reports tend to describe cornices, stairwells, and older masonry rather than dramatic collapses, and it is why Italy's building-survey program in the area has focused on cumulative vulnerability rather than any single event.

## Rising ground is not a countdown

Here is the part that deserves care, because it is where public understanding usually goes wrong.

Uplift is not a schedule. Campi Flegrei has been at the "yellow" attention level in Italy's four-tier volcanic alert system since 2012 — a designation that means monitoring has been intensified and parameters are being tracked closely, not that an eruption has been forecast. The system has three levels above yellow, and moving between them requires specific, agreed-upon changes in the data.

Researchers broadly work with two overlapping explanations for the current unrest, and the honest answer is that they are difficult to separate from the surface:

- **A hydrothermal interpretation.** Superheated water and gas — much of it originating from magma sitting several kilometers down — migrate into shallow rock, pressurize it, and lift it. This can produce years of uplift, gas emission, and shallow seismicity without magma itself rising to shallow depth.
- **A magmatic interpretation.** A body of magma at depth is intruding or degassing more actively, driving the same signals from below.

Both produce uplift. Both produce earthquakes. The discriminating evidence tends to come from gas chemistry, deformation patterns, and how the crust responds to repeated stress — and recent work has emphasized a third factor that complicates the picture: after decades of being stretched and shaken, the shallow crust here may simply be weaker than it was, meaning it fractures at lower stress than it used to. Under that reading, more frequent earthquakes are partly a sign of a fatigued lid, not necessarily a stronger push from beneath.

That is a genuinely important nuance, and it cuts both ways. It offers a less alarming explanation for rising quake counts. It also means the system's behavior is changing in ways that make historical analogies less reliable.

## The 1982–84 precedent

The last major bradyseismic crisis ran from 1982 to 1984 and lifted the ground at Pozzuoli by roughly 1.8 meters. Tens of thousands of residents were relocated; the old town core of Rione Terra was evacuated and stayed largely empty for years afterward. Then the ground stopped, settled somewhat, and the crisis ended without an eruption.

That is the most useful precedent available, and it points in a reassuring direction — sustained, meters-scale uplift ended quietly. But the current episode has now run far longer than that one, at a slower rate, and it is arriving in a place with two more generations of construction on top of it.

## What is being watched, and what would change the assessment

If you want to follow this the way monitoring agencies do, the meaningful indicators are not the magnitude headlines. They are:

- **Uplift rate**, measured in millimeters per month by GPS stations and satellite radar. Acceleration matters far more than the accumulated total.
- **Earthquake depth.** Persistent shallow activity fits the hydrothermal picture. A sustained migration of seismicity toward the surface, or new activity at intermediate depths, would be a different signal.
- **Gas chemistry** at the Solfatara and Pisciarelli fumarole fields — particularly the ratios of carbon dioxide to water vapor and helium isotopes, which help distinguish a magmatic contribution from a purely hydrothermal one.
- **Ground temperature and emission flux**, which track how much heat the system is moving.

None of those has a single threshold that flips a switch. Alert-level changes are made on a package of evidence by a national commission, not on any one reading.

## The practical layer

For residents and visitors, the operative guidance is unglamorous and comes from Italy's Civil Protection Department and municipal authorities, not from any article:

- Know whether your address falls in the designated hazard zones, and know the assigned assembly points and evacuation route — the local comune publishes them.
- Keep the standard earthquake habits: secure heavy furniture, know which interior wall or doorway you would move to, keep documents and medications somewhere you can grab them.
- Treat official channels as the source of truth during an event. Aftershock sequences in this caldera routinely produce a wave of speculation that outruns the data by hours.
- If a building has been posted as unusable after inspection, that assessment reflects strain that is not always visible from the street.

## The wider point

Campi Flegrei is a stress test for something more general than volcanology. It is what happens when a slow-moving natural hazard sits under a place people cannot simply leave — where the housing is old, the economy is local, the deadline is unknown, and the honest scientific answer is "we are monitoring it, and it may go on like this for years."

The port reopens. The households return or they don't. The instruments keep logging millimeters. Four and a half feet accumulated in twenty-one years is not a headline on any single day, which is precisely why it took a magnitude 4.7 to make anyone outside Naples look at it.

---

*This article summarizes publicly reported information and the current published scientific understanding of the Campi Flegrei caldera. Figures on damage, injuries, and displacement reflect initial official reports and are commonly revised. It is general information, not emergency guidance — for situation-specific instructions, follow Italy's Civil Protection Department and local municipal authorities.*
